Governments can set the environment. We have seen how bad management, runaway deficits, tax laws and a lack of understanding of the importance of investment can kill an economy.
The Progressive Conservative approach provides a clear change in that environment. It will lead to more economic growth and more jobs. The Liberal policies have led us into a zero-sum world. It is a world of factionism and mistrust; one man's gain is another man's loss. That is the fatal flaw of the message of the Prime Minister last week. He says that we must

October 27, 1982
The Economy
have trust and that we must be generous with our neighbours. But when people are struggling for survival, when people fear that they will lose their jobs or that their children cannot find that first job, there is not much trust and generosity. Rhetoric will not produce the harmony we all want, but a healthy economy will.
We must reject the zero-sum world of the Liberal Government. We must move in a new direction where Canadians are encouraged by a government which understands the value of risk investment, investment that will create jobs, a government which understands the importance of competent management, and a government which knows that security only comes with a healthy economy.
Last week Canadians in three ridings rejected the zero-sum world. These Canadians confirmed recent Gallup polls. Canadians want this new direction. Canadians want to be proud of our country. We were proud of our country in 1967, of our people, of our way of life, of our industries and of our position in the world community. But Canadians have been robbed of this pride in recent years by 15 years of neglect and mismanagement.
Hon. Members today must take the first steps to regaining that pride, that hope for the future, that opportunity to rebuild the country of which we were so proud 15 years ago. The Minister's statement is a start, but it is only a very small start; we must go much further.

Mr. Speaker, before I comment upon the observations of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) this afternoon, I should like to put this debate in the context of what the country is facing right now. Up to this point in 1982 we have had somewhere between 9,000 and
10,000	businesses which have gone bankrupt. In real numbers we have had something like one and three-quarter million Canadian men and women unemployed, people who would like to be obtaining cheques for working, not cheques from the Unemployment Insurance Commission or the welfare office. Because of the Liberal Government's total lack of concern with the seriousness of the economic situation, 1 want to indicate to the Minister that between now and Christmas we will have the loss of probably between 80,000 and 100,000 more jobs. Also we will have-and it is a conservative estimate-about 2,000 more businesses which will have gone bankrupt. Every region and every sector of the Canadian economy is affected by the recession that we are going through. That is the situation in which the Minister made his statement that went on for 25 or 27 pages.
What has the Minister come up with for the men and women who are looking for some hope? They are not looking for a pie in the sky or a quick fix. They want to believe that between now and Christmas there is some reason for economic hope; they are looking for that. What did the Minister come up with? I ask the Conservative critic to check his numbers. If he looks at the direct spending program and reads the fine print of the Minister, it is for 18 months, not 12 months the $500 million allocated for direct job creation would not even be adequate for 12 months. If we add the slight changes that were
made in housing spending to the changes in fiscal outlay which the Minister said we will now get for direct job creation, we will have a total, in an economy measured in billions of dollars, of $480 million being allocated for job creation. This will create at the most some 60,000 jobs. What we need in a crisis, because surely that is what we have, is a crisis program. In Canada right now we need a national recovery program, not the pittance thrown out by the Liberal Government this afternoon.
I will return to the Conservative Party in a minute, but all I can say at this point is that if cliches were a substitute for policy, we certainly heard them from the group on my right today. Having said that we must address those concerns, I want to underline it for those of us who have jobs. For some of us in the House of Commons they will be temporary jobs, I am convinced, but those of us who are working must consider the effects of the unemployment crisis. Michael Harrington of the United States wrote a book a number of years ago about the hidden poor. In a human sense we have in Canada the hidden unemployed. There is a great tendency for us to think in this land of ours that because we have unemployment insurance and the social fabric of the welfare state, not completed but at least in place in a way that it was not in the 1930s, somehow the men and women who are unemployed are not really suffering. There are Hon. Members on all sides of the House who have talked to the unemployed, but I do not know if there are Cabinet Members who have done so. The kind of unemployment we are experiencing now has a corrosive effect on the affected people, of which anyone who is at all sensitive is fully aware.
Men and women in this country want jobs, as we have said on other occasions. It is true that they want jobs; they do not want handouts. They do not want from their national Government 25 or 27 pages of so-called analysis. They would like to see a 25-page program which could be implemented now; that is what they want. There is a human concern out there which we must address. It is very real. Rather than coming up with a Program which is a drop in the bucket in the short run of less than $500 million, we are proposing a spending Program in the short run of more than four times that amount. We do so and do not hesitate to do so. If the Tories are afraid to mention dollars because of some kind of perceived backlash, I can say that we in this Party are not afraid to talk about the need for spending to meet a human requirement right now-to create jobs. We say that by spending $2.2 billion, using the same multiplier the Minister used in his figures earlier today, we would be able to create a minimum of 250,000 jobs for the men and women who need them.
Again unlike the Liberals and unlike the party on my right we are prepared to say concretely that those who are in a position to help pay now should be out there in the front of the line with their pay cheques, because the time for rhetoric about
October 27, 1982

justice, the time for rhetoric about caring and the time for rhetoric about co-operation is over. It is time to start implementing the socially desirable goal right now.
Therefore, we are prepared to say-and I did not hear the Tories talking about this nor did I hear it coming from the Liberals-that it was a social injustice of high proportions that we put a six and five wage and salary control guideline on the people in the federal public sector urged the provinces and urged the private sector to follow suit-which the Tories supported-and at the same time cut by over $ 1 billion the tax paid by the wealthiest people in this country. That is a disgrace.
We say there is a source of revenue.

Another illusion, says a Tory. 1 say to the member who just spoke, after having heard the Tories' speech, there has been one Government in the world that has implemented the Canadian Progressive Conservative Party's program and that is the Government of Margaret Thatcher. Britain's unemployment rate has risen 38 months in a row under Margaret Thatcher, and the same thing would come from the Tories here.
We say that if we need money to create jobs, we are prepared to start practising a little of the equity that other parties talk about. We would rescind the tax cut that was provided by the Liberals last fall for upper income Canadians, and we would say "Yes, indeed, if workers are going to be holding down their incomes to six and five and if pensioners in this country are going to pay income tax, then it is time to put a surtax on upper income Canadians to get money to help create jobs that are needed now."
At the same time we are saying that if the Government had looked with some imagination at federal spending programs- and again I did not hear any specifics from the Tories-it would find that there are areas in which cuts could take place that under normal times I say would not necessarily have to be cut at all. If, however, there are areas of federal Government spending that do not have as their leading priority job creation, then we in this party say that many of those areas should be cut out, and we do not hesitate to say it.
Therefore, in this context we have proposed that the planning under way to spend money on embassies abroad in the coming year be cut. Also, of money that is being spent in the National Unity Information office we say that one-third of the over-all budget which the Government allocates for publicity for its programs could be cut. If we did that, we would have a saving in public spending already allocated of some $400 million, and $1.3 million would come from surtax.
Finally, we would take another program introduced by the Minister. I see the Minister questions the surtax figures, but we have checked and double checked, and we stand by our figures. I say to the Minister that his department is the last in this country that should try to correct anybody else's figures at this time.

I come to another proposal. It came in last fall's budget which came from the Minister who was then the minister of energy. He provided a special kind of handout to the oil companies. I refer to the PIP grants. We said at that time when we voted against them-the Tories, of course, voted for them-that it would lead to irrational investment. We said that, if we wanted to Canadianize the oil industry, we should do it as do most other energy producing countries in the world, that is, use the public sector to do it and not the taxpayers' money to finance private investment. We voted against that Program.

I tell my hon. friend to check the voting record. We voted against it, not only because we have a public instrument which we say is a better way of dealing with the energy sector, but also because we said it would lead to irrational investment, even if you wanted to go the private sector route.

If the Tories would calm down, I will tell them something about what happened. They should know, among others because I have heard some of them complain, that a monumental disaster occurred, the biggest private disaster in Canada since the Second World War. I am speaking of the Dome Petroleum situation. That bail-out, which was inappropriate, was the direct result of this Government's program, supported by the Tories. We say to that cut that out.
We say that if the Government will not cut it out, at least let it give us $500 million out of it and put that money into direct job creation.
I want to say something now about the way we will spend the money. We have the naive view on this side of the House, unlike the Party to my right, literally, figuratively, and in every other way, that an opposition Party, particularly at this point in our history, has an obligation to say what we would do. That is an obligation.
You have not had a single idea.

We would take this money now, recognizing that there is unemployment from British Columbia in the west to Newfoundland in the east, and put some $220 million into reforestation programs that will not be "make work" but would do for our reforestry what western Europe has done for its forests for decades, that is to manage forests in a sensible way so that when the market picks up in very significant proportions at the turn of the century in the United States, we will have the trees to service the market. In short, we could create jobs now for an immediate benefit, but also we would have a long-run economic benefit for our forests. That makes sense.
Similarly, we would not put the pittance in housing which the Minister has talked about; we would immediately inject some $500 million into housing to create more jobs in many

sectors of the economy. In particular, we would deal with those one-industry towns, normally in the resource sector, that are so terribly affected now, whole communities like Port Alberni, like Sudbury, like Faro in the Yukon, like Rouyn-Noranda in Quebec, like Bathurst, and like the Miramichi region in New Brunswick. I am talking about communities totally dependent upon one sector of the economy that are now experiencing horrific social consequences as a result of this recession.
In the short run we would allocate part of the moneys that I have just talked about to these communities. On behalf of my colleagues, starting on Friday in Sudbury I will be announcing very specifically what can be done in one-industry towns where there is a crisis problem now. Things can be done Mr. Speaker, and I looked for a little imaginative action coming from the Minister on that side of the House about what can be done for these communities.
Another example is the situation concerning the fisheries on both coasts. We would use part of the money for fishery enhancement programs that many Members on all sides of the House have talked about. We in this party believe money should be allocated for that purpose now.
These are just some of the areas and sectors on which in the short run we think money should now be spent to create jobs that are badly needed by men and women, young and old, who want to work.
But having said that, what we have heard from the new Minister of Finance is just a repetition of his predecessor's crisis management, just stumbling from one situation to another. If the short run program is so in adequate, in human or in economic terms, as I think it is, then I ask you, what about the long run? Here is a Minister who used to pride himself in trying at least to address the long-run interests of the country. There were a number of aspects of the National Energy Program which this party supported because some contents in that program did have the long run in mind. I want to say that he, as Minister if Finance, has revealed himself as the ultimate Liberal once again, because we have no perspective at all of what lies beyond the end of this year, let alone beyond the next election.
In the next couple of minutes I want to address an unstated assumption, both by this Minister in his presentation today and also by the Conservative Party to my right, because I think it is a very serious one. The unstated assumption is really that the marketplace must be relied upon to get us out of our very difficult situation.

One of the Conservative Members says, "Good idea!". I would ask that hon. member to compare what has been happening in Great Britain for the past 38 months with what has been happening in other western European countries. Only one country has had 38 months of perpetual
increase in unemployment. That has been under Margaret Thatcher, because she has relied entirely upon the marketplace. That is what happened.
Through Your Honour I want to urge the people of our land, particularly right now, to think historical terms and to keep in mind that this not 1932, it is 1982. Much has gone on in other countries in the world in the past 50 years. If the Party to my right wants to take us back in history and if the Liberal Party is already doing that, they can go that route. There is one Party in this land that believes we should learn a little from history and from what is going on in other countries so that we can create a country which will be decent and exciting in the future. We do not want the past.

Therefore, I would ask a rhetorical question of my friends in the Conservative Party and in the Liberal Party opposite as individuals. Many are friends in this House even though we have profound differences about policy. I would ask them to really think about what they are saying and to consider whether it has been our overwhelming emphasis on the private sector alone in this country in the last 30 to 35 years which has got us into a situation where we do indeed have low productivity, where we are not carrying out research and development, where "management in this part of the world, unlike western Europe and unlike Japan, is too preoccupied with the short-run buck, not enough concerned with long-run investment". I do not quote from a socialist source but, rather, from the Harvard Business Review.
If the private sector alone has created this mess that we are now in, why, in heaven's name, should we turn back to the private sector to get us out of the mess? That is the question.

Therefore, we in this party, like the Social Democrat movement in western Europe, would ask a question. There is not a country in western Europe with a Social Democrat Government which has an unemployment level which is even half of ours. I ask the Minister, and maybe he should ask the question: why is it that West Germany, Sweden, Norway and Denmark which, of course, are having difficulties now, have unemployment levels which are less than half our level?
I now come to the substantive point which I wanted to make to the Minister. He should understand it. I wish he would only act upon it. The point is that these societies in western Europe learned from the Depression. Overwhelmingly, they had Social Democratic Governments. However, there is another country on the other side of the Pacific Ocean, Japan, which has not a social democratic government. I say to the Minister and to the Tories that there is no major economic decision made in that country called Japan without the full involvement of the Government of Japan. The Japanese know what they are doing. They do not rely on the unfettered results of the marketplace.

1 say that what distinguishes us as a party from the Conservatives and the Liberals is that we want to deal with realities. We do not want to deal with myths about private enterprise. We want to deal with the reality of facing our mixed economy now, in 1982, because that is what it is, and finally to make it work for the people of Canada. We want to make changes to achieve that. Specifically, we say it is necessary that the federal Government show a little leadership. God knows, it has made bad decisions in the past. We should have a government which should commit itself to a plan for the future. It should consult with the Provinces, by all means, in a federal state. That is essential. It should consult with labour and with the private sector. But then, like the leading nations in western Europe, like Japan, the federal Government, the Cabinet, should bring before the Parliament of Canada a development plan for this nation and should say, "Over the next decade, this is where the money will go to create long term jobs for the people of Canada". That was totally lacking, of course, in the approach of the Minister today.
I want to say that we were not only concerned about the inadequacies of the short run and long run programs. What was more alarming in the sense of equity was the proposal to increase the U1C premiums. As I said, during the past year the Government cut the taxes of the richest people in our land by over a billion dollars. The Government has imposed a six and five guideline program on the working people of Canada at the same time. The Government reduces the cost to the rich with one hand and increases the burdens of the workers with the other. That is what it did between last October and last August. But now what is the Government doing? It is coming along and saying to working people, men and women, "We will increase your premiums by 40 per cent".

And that of employers, yes, but I am not referring particularly to the people who got it in the neck so far this year. The Government will increase it by 40 per cent. This is not six and five, which the Government keeps preaching. This is not a 6 per cent increase or a 5 per cent increase. It is more than a 6 per cent times 5 per cent increase. It is a 40 per cent increase. We must keep it in mind that this is really a form of taxation.
It was not recommended by the labour movement, Mr. Minister, and you can check your records on that. I listened to the Minister's wording with care. He said that he had consulted labour and management. I say, through Your Honour, that the Minister did not say that labour supported it, because he knows darned well that no labour movement in this country would accept such a regressive tax as a 40 per cent increase on the premiums paid by ordinary workers.

1 do not think Your Honour could have a better example of the hypocrisy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) than what we heard last week when he spoke of the need for fairness. I think one of the wonderful phrases was that
The Economy
the strong must help the weak. Of course, we reject the notion that unemployed men and women workers should seem to be the weak. They are unfortunate citizens who are out of work because we have not managed our economy appropriately. Surely we have had enough of this hypocritical rhetoric. If the Government of Canada is bringing in what can only be described in historical terms as a reactionary program, as a program which wants to take us back in the form of economic decision-making to a distant past, to take us back to a distribution of income which was inequitable and is becoming more inequitable, then for God's sake at least spare us the rhetoric about justice and co-operation. If the Government Members are to be reactionary, let them be honest reactionaries like those in the Party to my right.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I believe the Minister set out eight different items that he was withdrawing from the November budget. However, he did not make any change in two key areas. In particular because of the significance of the economic impact, why did the Minister avoid making a change in the capital cost allowance, which has clearly had an impact on reducing the level of investment in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, obviously there are a number of areas where additional changes could have been made. All would have had significant impact on increasing the Government deficit and loss of revenue.
I examined this particular issue very carefully. I found that the changes which had been proposed are quite appropriate, and I support them.

Investment activity creates revenue because it creates jobs. It provides people with employment and takes people off of the unemployment rolls. Surely, when the Minister was making that decision, he could have taken into account the revenue-generating impact on that and reinstated that particular credit because of its impact on job creation. Could he answer the question in the context in the investmentgenerating impact and the job creating impact?

Again, one could decide to abolish the corporate income tax completely and decide that the companies will use the money for all kinds of good purposes for creating investment and jobs. One could do the same with personal income tax. People would find all kinds of uses for the money they would be left with. However, as long as you have a state, you have taxation, expenses and public programs. You need to raise funds.
In this particular instance, the Capital Cost Allowance is one of those benefits that could be adjusted, and this is what we have done. I completely support what my predecessor has done in that regard.

(Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, ! also have a question specifically relating to the program which the Minister has entitled the New Employment Expansion and Development Program, the NEED Program. I believe that most of us would have understood what the Minister was saying if he had said that the allocation of the $500 million was to create
60,000	jobs over one year. My question relates to the source of his data, that he could look after that need by creating 60,000 jobs over 18 months.
As 1 understand the rule of thumb used by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axwortny), the Government would have been at least technically in a position of having to create 60,000 over a 12 month period, not over an 18 month period. I am conerned that the Minister's data is faulty and therefore the allocation of funds will not be sufficient for the so-called exhaustees between now and June.

The Minister of Employment and Immigration will be available to answer specific questions on that particular Program. I just want to point out that it will take a few months, first of all, to gear up the Program. We have to have consultations before the Program can begin to be implemented. The money is proposed today but I doubt funds will be available to start before the beginning of 1983.
Therefore, when you are calculating the time of this announcement and the time that the Program will come into effect, I think this adds a few months to the Program. 1 suspect that this is the reason why this period has been mentioned.
In addition, there are some expenditures that are incurred after the Program is technically terminated in the sense that you are not starting new projects, for instance. Even after the Program is stopped some projects still continue for a few months because they have come in before and are, let us say, three, four or five month programs.
I suspect the total expenditure of the Programs will be spread over 18 months, but 1 will ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to address this particular situation and provide the Hon. Member with more specific information.

My supplementary question relates to part of the problem he described in his answer. That is, when a program is gearing up he knows that between now and the end of the year more people coming off the unemployment insurance benefits will be going on welfare. The Minister indicated on page 14 of his statement this afternoon that he was going to have further consultations with business, labour and other parties. I wonder whether or not that included any discussions with provinces and municipalities with respect to any change in the Government's contributions under the Canada Assistance Plan which could assist municipalities with respect to welfare payouts?

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: The Minister announced that the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Program will only apply to first-time buyers of new houses as of next January. I can understand that in some respect because only 22,400 of the 63,000 applications taken up so far have applied to new houses. My concern is that Mr. Lortie, in his recommendations, recommended against the mortgage reduction scheme because it would apply only to new houses and would hence have a distorting effect on the marketplace. How will the Minister get around the distortion of the marketplace, which I think will happen, if he applies the Home Ownership Stimulation Plan as of January to new houses only and not to first-time home buyers?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member would have a very good point indeed if it was a permanent program, something that would be in operation for all time where one would have that kind of distortion in favour of housing at the expense of other allocation resources. But this is a short-term program. It will expire at the end of April. It is aimed at stimulating a sector of the economy that is extremely weak at the present time and which, as the Hon. Member knows, has significant impact in terms of tertiary job creation.
This is the reason why the program is continued, in order to try to prime up this particular sector which has been very weak this year indeed.
I agree with him that if this were a permanent program it would have the impact which he has mentioned. However, on the basis of a short-term program, to inject funds and encourage the consumer to buy new houses, we think this is a valid approach.
I would also say that, looking at the decline in interest rates which has taken place since June, and looking at the fact that the price of houses has declined on an average across the country, I would hope that we will see a resurgence of activity and that house builders will get into business. Inventory of new houses has been drawn back in the last few months. I hope that we will see a serious rise in that sector.

We can only hope that the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is not taking his advice from the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove), the former Minister responsible for housing. We know the disastrous consequences of that.
Can the Minister tell us why he is proceeding with the Canada Rental Supply Plan? As the Minister knows, of the
30,000	units permitted for the Canada Rental Supply Plan in the last budget, less than 25 per cent have been taken up thus far. He made no provision for co-op housing. We are facing a problem of affordability. Housing starts are down. That speaks to availability. They were down into the 80,000 bracket in September and August. Why did the Minister not re-direct the money that is going into the Canada Rental Supply Plan, which has not been taken up across the country, and put that into co-op housing where there is immediate demand for
October 27, 1982

low-cost housing and which would provide a quick fix in terms of housing starts?
I will be giving serious consideration to the suggestion put forward by my friend. 1 will examine this particular situation. I thank him for drawing it to my attention.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest when the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) was commenting on the six and five program and the fact that a great deal of concern on behalf of the Government is still over the question of inflation. I want to deal with an area which is very close to him because of his previous experience, the question of energy. Considering that the cost that Canadians will experience in the year ahead will certainly have a very definite impact on the rate of inflation in this country, when an increase in the price of energy has such an incredible effect when you consider a country as vast as Canada, will the Minister comment on his thoughts about re-entering negotiations with the producing Provinces in an effort to put a cap on the increases anticipated in the months ahead that will result in a number of percentage points increase in the rate of inflation?

Mr. Speaker, having lived through that experience for a year and a half, particularly before reaching an agreement, I think I would invite my hon. friend to go ahead as an explorer. I would be very happy to give him letters of introduction to the various Ministers of Energy in the various producing Provinces. If he has some success, I will be ready to give him credit for that success.
Frankly, we have a firm agreement with the producing Provinces. Those agreements provide for adjustments in the price of energy, oil and gas in particular. In Canada we are still in a situation of catching up with the international prices for oil and gas. We will end up in a situation where for oil discovered before 1981, we will pay 75 per cent of the international price by next July when we have reached the ceiling. Therefore, we in Canada are benefiting. We have benefited and we will continue to benefit in Canada with oil and gas prices well below the international prices. Provincial taxes in particular have a significant impact from Province to Province, but fundamentally the price of oil and gas in this country will remain below the international prices, all over the country.
The solution is in trying to re-negotiate those contracts. Frankly, I do not think anybody would be well received in any of the provincial capitals concerned. I wish my hon. friend good luck if he wants to try his hand. If he has some success, I will put him in touch with the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). Maybe he will have great success.

Mr. Speaker, the western part of Canada, like all parts of Canada, is experiencing a devastation of the critical industry of forestry. I listened with interest to the statements tonight when the Minister commented on the extension of the

existing programs that presumably are to assist and stimulate the housing industry and, therefore, the forest industry as well. We know how successful these programs have been in stimulating housing construction across Canada as well as the forest industry and related manufacturing industry-not very impressive.
My question is, why would people in Canada, who are very concerned about the forest industry, feel encouraged by what the Minister has said tonight? From what I have been able to gather, he has not said anything new in areas that would assist that very critical Canadian industry.

On the forest industry, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to the Lion. Member that I have added to date $150 million for expenditures in the area of housing. Second, as the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) indicated, the change that I have made to the Home Ownership Stimulation Plan will be restricted after January 1 to new houses so that we will not have some of the takers who at the present time are just buying existing houses. As far as the forest and lumber industries are concerned, and I am sure the Hon. Member knows this as well as I do, one should not be under any illusion about what we can do in Canada in terms of the forest and lumber industry.
I was rather surprised to hear his Leader talking about this a few minutes ago. We know in effect that we could close all the lumber plants in Canada, with the exception of two in British Columbia, and that would be enough to supply the Canadian demand. In effect, quite clearly the forest industry in Canada will start a real recovery when the housing industry in the United States has its recovery. There will be a world demand for it.
We have a world-size industry in the forestry field. That will not be true only for housing starts in Canada, but we will be able to sustain the forest industry we now have. It will have to come from a worldwide recovery because we have a worldwide industry.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), first of all, of course, about the matter of trust which cropped up so often in his own speech and the television address of the Prime Minister last week, and I would also like to know how the minister can ask employers, and especially employees, to pay 40 per cent more for their unemployment insurance premiums while asking these same employees and employers to accept the 6 and 5 per cent formula or else be penalized. When I think about the just society we were promised, I wonder how the minister can see any equity in imposing the six and five formula at the same time as a 40 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums to the same employees.

I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am rather surprised at the reasoning of the hon. member. First, unem-

October 27, 1982
The Economy
ployment insurance is, as its name indicates, a form of insurance, and insurance premiums increase or decrease according to the risk factor. The hon. member owns a car. His automobile insurance will increase or decrease according to the risks incurred during the year. The premiums are not related to the 6 and 5 formula or to anything else; it is an insurance program. When we lowered insurance premiums in 1981, we brought them down to the level of 1975. We did not ask the workers to take pay cuts because their insurance premiums were lower. Their collective agreements were maintained and the workers did not reduce their salary demands because they could say that unemployment insurance was a different matter, an insurance plan. If there are fewer unemployed, our premiums decrease and if there are more, our premiums increase. It is a simple as that and it has nothing to do with the 6 and 5 formula. Moreover, the hon. member says that we are now increasing the premiums by 40 per cent. What he forgets to mention is that the government of Canada has absorbed 60 per cent of the increase, which means that if all the Canadians are willing to contribute, the government will not increase taxes and will borrow $1 billion to help both businesses and workers so that they will have to pay only 40 per cent and not 100 per cent of the amount as provided under the unemployment insurance scheme. As I noted earlier, the Unemployment Insurance Commission, which includes representatives of labour and management, has specifically recommended the increase I have implemented. I believe that it is a matter of equity. The hon. member speaks about social justice and this is a very good example of social justice, since those who work share with those who are unemployed, and moreover, the government absorbs 60 per cent of the costs of this increase, which the employers and the employees would have to bear if the act were strictly applied.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). It involves the statement that he supported the income tax measures from the other two budgets that he has not addressed in his new budget. Several of these measures involve the concept which Canadians find unacceptable of taxing deemed income. For instance, the Minister did not address the issue of taxing capital gains reserves, although in many cases, particularly in farming communities to which he referred in his own background, farmers are taxed on money they do not have in their hands. Does he mean to imply in his statement that he
supports the measures he has not addressed, that he is continuing to support the concept of taxing deemed income or taxing money that people do not have in their hands?
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to a budget. I have not made a budget statement today.
